```{r}
#| label: setup
#| cache: false

pacman::p_load(targets, tidyverse, here, scales)

here::i_am("slides/pacific_pitch.qmd")
tar_config_set(store = here("_targets"))

source(here("R/tt_theme.R"))
source(here("R/malay_consistency.R"))
source(here("R/tax_shock_report.R"))
source(here("R/local_projections.R"))
source(here("R/pacific_coverage.R"))

theme_set(theme_minimal())

# Rendering is read-only: tar_read only, never tar_make.
tax_shocks  <- tryCatch(tar_read(tax_shocks),           error = \(e) tibble::tibble())
lp_cit      <- tryCatch(tar_read(lp_results_cit_event_effective), error = \(e) tibble::tibble())
lp_pooled   <- tryCatch(tar_read(lp_results_effective),           error = \(e) tibble::tibble())
coverage    <- tryCatch(tar_read(pacific_coverage),     error = \(e) tibble::tibble())

# Held back pending the C2a/C2b re-run (docs/deltas.md 2026-08-05). Same list as
# the `lp_shocks_*` targets, so both figures describe the same events.
deck_excluded <- c("MY-CIT-08", "MY-CIT-09", "MY-PIT-01", "MY-PIT-06")

have_shocks   <- nrow(tax_shocks) > 0
have_lp       <- nrow(lp_cit) > 0
have_coverage <- nrow(coverage) > 0
```

## Malaysia: every statutory tax change, read from the budget speech that announced it

```{r}
#| label: tax-events
#| eval: !expr have_shocks
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5.0

plot_tax_events_slide(tax_shocks, exclude_ids = deck_excluded,
                      timing = "effective", base_size = 15)
```

::: {.notes}
Corporate, personal and consumption tax changes, 1980-2019, identified from
Malaysian primary-source budget documents by the LLM pipeline and stamped by a
human reviewer. Bar height is the statutory rate change in percentage points;
hollow markers are acts with no headline rate change (regime introductions,
one-off levies). Colour is the pipeline's exogeneity verdict: was the change
motivated by something other than the current state of the economy.

Every event traces back to a quoted passage in a named document. That chain is
what let a reviewer's objection to two corporate-tax rows surface a machinery
defect earlier this year.
:::

## Local projections from a single country are suggestive at most

```{r}
#| label: lp-irf
#| eval: !expr have_lp
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.6

plot_lp_irf(
  lp_cit, band = "exo",
  variant_labels = c(all = "All corporate rate cuts",
                     exo = "Exogenous corporate rate cuts"),
  y_lab = "Response to one corporate rate cut",
  base_size = 15
)
```

::: {.notes}
Local projections (Jorda 2005) of each outcome on Malaysian statutory corporate
income tax cuts, annual, 1980-2019, dated by the year the change took effect.
Shaded band is 90%, Newey-West. Six rate-bearing CIT acts fall in the window;
five are classified exogenous. The two lines differ by exactly one act: the 1998
Asian-crisis cut, which the pipeline classifies COUNTERCYCLICAL.

HOW TO READ THE SIGN. In the source data a rate cut is a negative number:
delta_pp is rate_to minus rate_from, so 28% to 27% is -1. The shock enters as
minus that, so a cut is a positive shock. Every coefficient on this slide is
therefore the response to a corporate rate CUT, and a positive value means the
outcome is higher after a cut - that is, expansionary. A negative value means
the outcome is lower after a cut.

THE UNITS ARE NOT THE SAME ACROSS PANELS, which is why they are on the strips
rather than the axis. Real GDP enters as 100 x log, so its numbers are
cumulative percent deviations of the level of GDP. Private investment and FDI
are already ratios to GDP measured in percent, so their numbers are percentage
points of GDP. The dependent variable is the outcome at t+h minus the outcome
at t-1, so every point is cumulative from the year before the change and
horizon 0 is the impact year.

THE SHOCK IS AN EVENT INDICATOR, NOT A SIZE. Each cut counts once regardless of
how many percentage points it moved, so these are average responses per cut, not
per percentage point. We began with a percentage-point shock and abandoned it:
the five exogenous cuts take only two sizes, 2pp in 1994-95 and 1pp across
2007-09, and those sizes line up with the eras they fell in - the tail of the
1990s boom and the global financial crisis. A continuous specification then
measures the gap between two decades and reports it as a dose-response. It
returned +3.2% of GDP per percentage point, which is roughly an order of
magnitude too large. Removing the size information removes that confound.

NO SYMMETRY CLAIM. All five exogenous events are cuts, so nothing here speaks to
what a rate increase would do.

WHAT THE SLIDE CLAIMS, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. The grey line includes the one cut
that was made because output was collapsing, and it runs sharply negative
(-4.5% of GDP on impact). The blue line removes that single act and the estimate
moves to roughly zero (-0.7% on impact, +1.5% by year two, t = 0.23). So the
claim is about the direction and size of the bias that endogenous events
introduce, and about the fact that removing them leaves an answer we cannot
distinguish from nothing. It is not a finding that corporate tax cuts raise
output in Malaysia. Nothing on this slide is statistically significant except
the FDI panel, where both lines are negative and we treat the result as
unresolved rather than as evidence.

Three of the five exogenous cuts take effect in 2007-09, so the short-horizon
response partly reflects the crisis and its rebound. No crisis control is added,
because that would be a specification choice made after seeing the result.

ROBUSTNESS. Pooling all three instruments instead - corporate, personal and
consumption, 8 exogenous event-years - gives a GDP response of +0.67% at horizon
2 that is stable whether or not magnitude is used. That pooled series mixes
percentage points across different tax bases, which is why it is not the
headline, but it is the more identified of the two.

This is the argument for the regional programme rather than against the method.
The pipeline produced a usable regressor from primary documents; one country's
corporate-tax record is simply too short to estimate a response from. More
countries is the fix.
:::

## The Pacific is in the growth data, and in no fiscal-shock dataset

```{r}
#| label: coverage
#| eval: !expr have_coverage
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5.0

plot_pacific_coverage(coverage, base_size = 15)
```

::: {.notes}
Years of usable data per country, 1990-2019, in the compiled cross-country panel
this project benchmarks against - the same statutory-rate series used by the
published cross-country procyclicality literature.

Eight of the ten Pacific countries in the panel have three decades of real GDP
and FDI and zero years of statutory tax-rate data. Samoa, Palau, the Cook
Islands and Nauru are not in the panel at all. Fiji and Papua New Guinea are the
only exceptions.

These countries therefore appear in every cross-country growth study and in no
fiscal-shock study. That is not because nobody wants the evidence; it is because
the documents have never been read. The Malaysia pilot shows the reading can now
be done in weeks rather than months, and most Pacific budget documents are in
English, so the corpus cost is below Malaysia's bilingual case.

What the funding buys: the cross-country variation that turns the middle slide
from a sign into a magnitude.
:::
